reason: The sources provide abundant, multi-sourced documentation confirming the 1946 V-2 No. 13 mission that captured Earth's first photo from space.
story: In October 1946, more than a decade before Sputnik, American researchers bolted a modified 35-millimeter newsreel camera into the nose of a captured German V-2 rocket at White Sands, New Mexico. Fired straight up, the repurposed ballistic missile climbed 65 miles above the desert, crossing the threshold of space and reaching five times higher than any previous photograph. Snapping a frame every second and a half, the camera captured the curving horizon of Earth framed against the pure blackness of outer space. With no parachute, the rocket plunged back down and slammed into the desert floor at high speed, obliterating the airframe. But the heavy steel cassette shielding the film survived intact. When researchers retrieved the canister and developed the frames that night, humanity saw Earth from beyond the atmosphere for the very first time—delivered not by a spacecraft, but by a salvaged weapon of war.
angle: The first photograph of Earth from outer space was taken not by a satellite, but by a captured Nazi ballistic missile crashing into the desert in 1946.

claims.claim: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket launched from White Sands, New Mexico, captured the first photograph of Earth from outer space.
The specific rocket that captured the image was designated V-2 No. 13.
The rocket ascended to a maximum altitude of roughly 65 miles (104 to 105 kilometers) above Earth.
The rocket's altitude placed it above the 100-kilometer boundary often recognized as the edge of space.
The photographs were captured using a modified 35-millimeter DeVry motion-picture camera.
The camera system was modified and developed by Clyde Holliday of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.
The camera was configured to expose one frame every 1.5 seconds during flight.
The images revealed Earth's curved horizon set against the blackness of space.
The rocket was not designed for a gentle landing and crashed into the desert upon descent, destroying the airframe.
The exposed film negative survived the violent impact protected inside a steel cassette.
Prior to this launch, the highest photograph of Earth had been taken from the Explorer II balloon in 1935 at an altitude of 13.7 miles (22 km).
The V-2 camera reached roughly five times the altitude of the 1935 Explorer II balloon flight.
The V-2 rocket was originally developed by Nazi Germany during World War II as a long-range ballistic missile.
Thousands of forced laborers died during the manufacture of V-2 rockets in the underground Mittelwerk tunnels.
After Germany was defeated in 1945, captured V-2 components were shipped to the United States for research and testing.
In a 1950 National Geographic article, Clyde Holliday wrote that the photos showed how Earth would look to visitors from another planet on a spaceship.
The flight took place more than a decade before Sputnik 1 became the first artificial satellite in orbit.

disputed: Impact speed of the descending rocket: S2 quotes 500 feet per second, S6 cites NASA data stating over 340 miles per hour, while S3 notes reconstructions cite 150 meters per second and disputes exaggerated claims of 500 to 800 meters per second. Scripts should describe the crash as high speed or attribute the exact rate.

Condition of the camera body: S2, S4, and S6 report the camera was smashed or shattered on impact, whereas S3 states some recovery accounts describe it as usable except for damage like a missing lens. Scripts should emphasize that the steel film cassette protected the film while the vehicle wrecked.

Payload equipment configuration: S7 mentions eight movie cameras in the instrument package, while other sources focus on the single 35mm DeVry movie camera. Scripts should refer specifically to the 35mm DeVry camera that produced the surviving space photographs.
